title: What If... We Let Ourselves Imagine Again?
subtitle: Because resistance alone won’t build what comes next.
html:
Still Here → What If…

For the last few weeks, Still Here has served as a kind of warning siren—a series of dispatches from the edge of something we once thought couldn’t happen here.

I haven’t just been tracking headlines. I’ve been tracing something quieter. Heavier.

The shift in feeling.

The ambient numbness.

The silence where outrage used to live.

But at some point, the question becomes:

Now what?

What do we do after we’ve named the danger?

Why This Shift—Why Now

Because warnings don’t build.

They’re necessary—but incomplete.

We need vision. Not just vigilance.

Direction, not just resistance.

And if I’m honest, I think a lot of us are tired—of reacting, of bracing, of narrating collapse like it’s the only story left to tell.

So I’m starting something new.

It’s called “What If…”

And it’s not an escape from reality.

It’s a return to the part of it we still get to shape.

What to Expect

Short, grounded glimpses of the kind of country we could live in—if we pulled the right levers.

A thought experiment.

A provocation.

A reintroduction to imagination.

This doesn’t start with re-search on a preconceived laundry list of “problems to solve”.

It starts with the search itself — for a vision the tomorrow we want to create together.

  • What if AI profits helped pay for the livelihoods of those they displace?

  • What if your kid’s teacher didn’t have to work a second job to get by?

  • What if your medical check-up was free—because the wealth your data created came back around?

  • What if “public infrastructure” meant not just roads and bridges, but dignity, care, and peace of mind?

Each piece will tell a small story—rooted in real leverage points—of how we might bend the system without breaking ourselves in the process.

It’s Not About Being Right

This series isn’t about enforcing one vision of the future.

It’s about reclaiming the right to imagine one—together.

Because if we don’t?

The only futures on offer will come from those who profit from collapse.

One Last Thing

If you’ve read Still Here up to this point—thank you.

If you’ve shared a post, forwarded an essay, or just sat with the discomfort—I’m grateful.

But this next chapter is different.

It’s not just about staying awake.

It’s not even just about remaining human.

It’s about — together — becoming more humane.

Let’s ask better questions.

Let’s remember that imagining something better isn’t naive.

Let’s find the hinges that make those imaginings real.

This is how transformation begins.

With gratitude,
Ari

title: The Future of Labor
subtitle: What If... Work Actually Worked for Us?
html:
It's been three months since I've written anything for Still Here…

Three months since the "What If..." series launched with the promise to shift from warning to wonder, from resistance to vision.

Why the silence?

Partly because the very system I'm about to critique has been consuming every ounce of creative energy I have. But mostly because watching the authoritarian moves of Trump's second administration unfold—the mass deportations, the weaponization of federal agencies, the systematic dismantling of democratic norms—has felt so urgent that I began to question whether imagining what comes next would be frivolous.

But here's where I've (re)-landed: Vision isn't frivolous. It's the way through.

We can't just resist our way out of authoritarianism. We have to build our way beyond it. We need something to rise for, not just against. We need to remember what we're defending and expand what we're fighting to create.

This series isn't about escaping reality—it's about preparing for the world we'll build when this moment passes. And it will pass. It must.

So let's start with something fundamental. Something that touches every single one of our lives every single day. Work.

You leave the office at 2 PM on a Tuesday.

Not because you're sick. Not because of a family emergency. Not because you're sneaking out early.

Because your work is done.

The project that needed your particular combination of creativity, analysis, and care—it's complete. Tomorrow, you'll start something new. But today? Today, you get to pick up your kids from school. You get to take that pottery class. You get to write that essay you've been thinking about for months.

This isn't fantasy. This is what work looks like when it's designed for humans instead of extracting from them.

As I said, this piece comes three months after my last one—not because I ran out of ideas, but because work consumed every ounce of creative energy I had. The system that I'm critiquing has been extracting my capacity to critique it.

The irony would be funny if it weren't so common.

The Broken Promise

For millennia, work was straightforward: we toiled because survival demanded it. We hunted, gathered, farmed, built shelter. The sweat was honest—we worked because we had to, and we knew why.

Then came the promise of technology: machines would free us from drudgery. Computers would eliminate tedious tasks. Automation would give us back our time. We'd finally be liberated to pursue what makes us human—creativity, connection, meaning.

Instead, we got something else entirely.

We gained convenience and perhaps security, but we traded our autonomy for it. We're more productive than ever, yet more depleted. We have devices that can summon anything we want in minutes, but we barely have time to want anything beyond work.

And now? Now we're living through the age of intelligence—where the very thing we thought made us uniquely human is being automated. Reasoning itself is becoming a commodity. While AI systems take on more and more of what we are needed for, we're told to work harder to keep up and prove our worth—or be left behind with nothing.

The Seduction of Suffering

There’s an old myth humanity has bought into: Meaningful work requires sacrifice. If you're not grinding, you're not growing. If you're not exhausted, you're not earning it.

I've bought this story. You probably have too. There's something almost religious about this narrative—the Protestant work ethic dressed up in startup culture clothing, now with a technological twist. We mistake depletion for dedication, busyness for purpose.

But here's the contradiction we're not supposed to notice: The people who profit most from our work are rarely the ones doing it. While you're optimizing your productivity, someone else is optimizing their extraction of it. While I'm too drained to write about systemic change, the system keeps humming along unchanged.

The house always wins—but we're not the house.

This is our inflection point. We can let the age of intelligence become another chapter in the story of technological promises betrayed—or we can finally ask the question we should have asked decades ago:

What if instead of asking "How do we make people more productive?" we asked "How do we make centuries of productive progress serve people?"

A Different Day

Picture this:

You wake up without an alarm because you went to bed when you were tired, not when you finally finished answering emails.

You work on something that genuinely needs your human insight—not because you're desperately trying to stay relevant in the age of AI, but because you're finally free to focus on what no algorithm can replicate: the kind of ethical discernment that comes from lived experience, the creative synthesis that emerges from inspiration, the emotional intelligence that grows from genuine care.

When algorithms do get better at something you used to do, you don't get fired. You get paid. Because the productivity gains from automation flow back to the communities that made them possible.

The result? You have energy left. Time to think. Space to care for the people you love and be cared for in return. Bandwidth for the projects that matter to you—the ones that might not make money but might change everything.

This isn't about working less—it's about work becoming more human.

The Infrastructure

What would it take to build such a world?

Resource Dividends: Every time productivity increases through automation, the gains get shared—not just with shareholders, but with the communities whose data trained the algorithms, whose jobs transformed, whose lives were affected.

Time Sovereignty: Maybe it's a 30-hour work week at first. Maybe 20 hours eventually. Maybe, as intelligence itself becomes automated, it's something we barely recognize as "work" at all. This isn't about being replaced by machines—it's about finally receiving the dividend from centuries of technological progress. The point: a functioning democracy requires citizens with time to think, participate, and care for each other.

Care as Real Work: The labor of raising children, caring for elders, maintaining communities—this is the foundation that makes all other work possible. What if we compensated it accordingly?

These aren't pipe dreams. They're policy choices that could free up people like us to do the work that actually matters.

Alaska—a deep red state—has been cutting annual dividend checks to every resident since 1982, funded by oil revenues extracted from land they collectively own. We could do the same with the data and attention harvested from our digital commons, or from the water used to power every interaction with ChatGPT. This is entirely achievable.

The Irony

There's a beautiful irony here: politicians campaign on "creating jobs" while most people secretly wish they didn't need their job to survive. We vote for more work while dreaming of less. What if we closed that gap?

France has a legal right to disconnect from work emails after hours. Iceland's four-day work week trials showed maintained productivity with dramatically improved worker wellbeing. Worker cooperatives like Spain's Mondragon prove enterprises can be both profitable and humane.

The tools exist. The models exist. What we lack isn't technology or economics—it's imagination and political pressure. And the time to wield it.

The Real Question

Right now, we're optimizing human life for economic productivity.

What if we optimized economic systems for human flourishing instead?

The question isn't whether we can afford to reorganize work around human needs.

The question is whether we can afford not to.

Because the current system isn't just extracting our labor—it's increasingly extracting our humanity. Our capacity for the very civic imagination we need to build something better.

The Next Conversation

If this resonates, it's probably because you're living some version of this contradiction too. You care about something beyond your paycheck, but your paycheck demands so much that the caring gets pushed to evenings and weekends—or never.

Meanwhile, we're living through the most profound technological shift in human history. The age of intelligence could finally deliver on technology's broken promises—or it could entrench the extraction even deeper.

The choice isn't being made in boardrooms or by algorithms. It's being made by us, in conversations like this one, in the visions we're willing to fight for.

What if you didn't have to choose between meaningful work and having time for meaning?

What if the future wasn't something that happened to us, but something we chose to build?

What if this inflection point became the moment we finally got technology right?

This is the first piece in the "What If..." series—exploring what becomes possible when we design systems for human flourishing rather than human extraction.

What would you like to see explored next?

title: "Prove Me Wrong": America's Addiction to Being Right
subtitle: ...and how it sabotages our hunger for connection and common ground.
html:
I don't usually write about individual tragedies—there are too many, and Charlie Kirk's assassination this week isn't more tragic than the school shooting that happened the same day, or the cascading crises continuing to unfold.

But there is too much to learn from this moment to let it simply pass. Kirk's life revealed what we're all craving—and his death revealed why we keep failing to find it.

Kirk's "Prove Me Wrong" slogan drew thousands of students, creating massive levels of engagement across our deepest divides. I disagreed strongly with virtually everything he said. I still believe much of his rhetoric was harmful in many ways.

But those packed auditoriums revealed something crucial:

We're desperate for clarity and connection—to make America make sense again—yet this hunger is sabotaged by our addiction to being right.

Charlie was tragically trapped in this very same dynamic.

What our culture is missing is a commitment to intellectual humility. You can see the trap in Kirk's own challenge: "Prove Me Wrong." Moral questions aren't math problems—you can't prove abortion is wrong the way you prove 2+2=4. But when you set up that kind of challenge, dialogue becomes impossible—no matter your intentions.

This approach, fragmented into bite-sized clips, turns moral complexity into the Thunderdome, and our systems reward exactly this kind of content. Algorithms and audiences crave ideological warfare. But when conversation becomes warfare, opponents become enemies to beat, conquer, eliminate. These are the tragic ends of a political culture built on winning and losing.1

Kirk was incredibly effective at driving engagement across divides—something the age of echo chambers desperately needs. But the lesson of this moment is that engagement alone isn't enough. We need it reframed constructively — urgently.

Not "prove me wrong," but "help me understand."

That's how we make sense of—and from—this senselessness.

1

The documentary Boys State offers a revealing window into how we systematically cultivate this combative political culture—through a program most Americans have never heard of, despite the remarkable number of political leaders who emerged from it. What was designed for a different political era now perpetuates a culture where those same dynamics have become counterproductive.
